questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question evaluates practical skills in per-tenant policy enforcement, dynamic configuration reload, and how a sidecar can drive access control using Kubernetes-native resources.

## Key Concepts
- Per-tenant ACLs loaded from ConfigMaps with tenant-specific naming conventions
- Dynamic config reload and conflict resolution between cluster-wide and namespace-scoped policies
- Sidecar architecture and policy evaluation pipeline
- Kubernetes ConfigMap watch mechanisms and Informers
- End-to-end testing within a single namespace

## Code Example
```yaml
# Example policy
tenant: tenant-a
rules:
  - path: /api/v1/users/*
    methods: ["GET","POST"]
  - path: /health
    methods: ["GET"]
```

## Implementation Details

### ConfigMap Structure
The sidecar watches ConfigMaps matching the pattern `cnf.acl.{tenant}.yaml` in the tenant's namespace. Namespace-scoped overrides follow the naming convention `cnf.acl.{tenant}.override.yaml`.

### Watch Mechanism
Use a Kubernetes Informer to watch ConfigMap changes. On update, the sidecar re-parses the YAML, merges policies (namespace overrides take precedence), and updates the in-memory rule engine without pod restart.

### Conflict Resolution
When cluster-wide and namespace-scoped policies conflict, apply a merge strategy where namespace-specific rules override cluster defaults for the same path and method combination. Log conflicts for observability.

### Testing Manifest
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: tenant-a-test
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: cnf.acl.tenant-a.yaml
  namespace: tenant-a-test
data:
  policy.yaml: |
    tenant: tenant-a
    rules:
      - path: /api/v1/users/*
        methods: ["GET", "POST"]
      - path: /health
        methods: ["GET"]
```

Validate by querying the /acl/status endpoint after applying the manifest to confirm rules are loaded correctly.

## Why This Is Asked
This question evaluates your ability to design end-to-end provenance controls for CNF environments, specifically addressing how key rotation impacts SBOM generation and policy enforcement in multi-tenant Kubernetes clusters.

## Key Concepts
- Cosign image signing with KMS-backed keys
- SPDX SBOM generation and attestation workflows
- Kyverno policy enforcement for signature and SBOM validation
- Key rotation impact on image provenance chains
- Namespace-scoped testing strategies and rollback procedures

## Code Example
```bash
# Sign image with KMS-backed key
cosign sign --key kms://mykms/path/to/key \
  --attachment sbom \
  registry.example.com/cnf:latest

# Generate and attach SBOM
syft registry.example.com/cnf:latest \
  -o spdx-json > sbom.spdx

cosign attest --key kms://mykms/path/to/key \
  --type spdx --predicate sbom.spdx \
  registry.example.com/cnf:latest
```

## Implementation Strategy
Deploy this solution progressively: start with image signing, add SBOM generation, implement Kyverno policies, then automate the key rotation workflow. Test in isolated namespaces before cluster-wide deployment.
